title: Caching Test Results
text: Caching Test Results As you learned in the related discussion, Go caches compiled packages if they haven’t changed. Go also caches test results when running tests across multiple packages if they have passed and their code hasn’t changed. The tests are recompiled and rerun if you change any file in the package or in the testdata directory. You can also force tests to always run if you pass the flag -count=1 to go test.

title: Capacity
text: Capacity As you’ve seen, a slice is a sequence of values. Each element in a slice is assigned to consecutive memory locations, which makes it quick to read or write these values. The length of a slice is the number of consecutive memory locations that have been assigned a value. Every slice also has a capacity, which is the number of consecutive memory locations reserved. This can be larger than the length. Each time you append to a slice, one or more values is added to the end of the slice. Each value added increases the length by one. When the length reaches the capacity, there’s no more room to put values. If you try to add additional values when the length equals the capacity, the append function uses the Go runtime to allocate a new backing array for the slice with a larger capacity. The values in the original backing array are copied to the new one, the new values are added to the end of the new backing array, and the slice is updated to refer to the new backing array. Finally, the updated slice is returned. The Go Runtime Every high-level language relies on a set of libraries to enable programs written in that language to run, and Go is no exception. The Go runtime provides services like memory allocation and garbage collection, concurrency support, networking, and implementations of built-in types and functions. The Go runtime is compiled into every Go binary. This is different from languages that use a virtual machine, which must be installed separately to allow programs written in those languages to function. Including the runtime in the binary makes it easier to distribute Go programs and avoids worries about compatibility issues between the runtime and the program. The drawback of including the runtime in the binary is that even the simplest Go program produces a binary that’s about 2 MB. When a slice grows via append , it takes time for the Go runtime to allocate new memory and copy the existing data from the old memory to the new. The old memory also needs to be garbage collected. For this reason, after the first allocation, the Go runtime increases a slice’s capacity by more than one each time it runs out of capacity. The amount of increase depends on the current capacity of the slice: current capacity new capacity 0 1 < 256 2 * current capacity >= 256 (current capacity + 768) / 4 This algorithm slowly converges at 25% growth (a slice with capacity of 512 will grow by 63%, but a slice with capacity 4,096 will grow by only 30%). Just as the built-in len function returns the current length of a slice, the built-in cap function returns the current capacity of a slice. It is used far less frequently than len . Most of the time, cap is used to check if a slice is large enough to hold new data, or if a call to make is needed to create a new slice. You can also pass an array to the cap function, but cap always returns the same value as len for arrays. Don’t put it in your code, but save this trick for Go trivia night. Let’s take a look at how adding elements to a slice changes the length and capacity. Run the code in Example 2-1 on The Go Playground. Example 2-1. Understanding capacity var x []int fmt.Println(x, len(x), cap(x)) x = append(x, 10) fmt.Println(x, len(x), cap(x)) x = append(x, 20) fmt.Println(x, len(x), cap(x)) x = append(x, 30) fmt.Println(x, len(x), cap(x)) x = append(x, 40) fmt.Println(x, len(x), cap(x)) x = append(x, 50) fmt.Println(x, len(x), cap(x)) When you build and run the code, you’ll see the following output. Notice how and when the capacity increases: [] 0 0 [10] 1 1 [10 20] 2 2 [10 20 30] 3 4 [10 20 30 40] 4 4 [10 20 30 40 50] 5 8 While it’s nice that slices grow automatically, it’s far more efficient to size them once. If you know how many things you plan to put into a slice, create it with the correct initial capacity. You do that with the make function.

title: Checking Your Code Coverage
text: Checking Your Code Coverage Code coverage is a very useful tool for knowing whether you’ve missed any obvious cases. However, reaching 100% code coverage doesn’t guarantee that there aren’t bugs in your code for some inputs. First you’ll see how go test displays code coverage and then you’ll look at the limitations of relying on code coverage alone. Adding the -cover flag to the go test command calculates coverage information and includes a summary in the test output. If you include a second flag -coverprofile, you can save the coverage information to a file. Let’s go back to the examples/table directory and gather code coverage information: $ go test -v -cover -coverprofile=c.out If you run your table test with code coverage, the test output now includes a line that indicates the amount of test code coverage, 87.5%. That’s good to know, but it’d be more useful if you could see what you missed. The cover tool included with Go generates an HTML representation of your source code with that information: $ go tool cover -html=c.out When you run it, your web browser opens and shows you a page with code coverage information using a dark mode color scheme. Every file that’s tested appears in the combo box in the upper left. The source code is in one of three colors. Gray is used for lines of code that aren’t testable, green is used for code that’s been covered by a test, and red is used for code that hasn’t been tested. This reliance on color is unfortunate for those who have red-green color blindness (and those whose publishers don’t want to print large blocks of black ink). To address this issue, I have created a fork of the cover tool. Install and run it with: $ go install github.com/jonbodner/coverlight@latest $ coverlight -html c.out The page that opens should look similar to Figure 6-1. Code with test coverage is displayed in black, code without test coverage is displayed as white text with a black background, and gray is used for untestable lines of code. From looking at this, you can see that you didn’t write a test to cover the default case, when a bad operator is passed to your function. Add that case to your slice of test cases: {"bad_op", 2, 2, "?", 0, &UnknownOpErr{Op: "?"}}, When you rerun go test -v -cover -coverprofile=c.out and coverlight -html c.out, you see in Figure 6-2 that the final line in DoMath is covered. There is still missing code coverage for the methods for UnknownOppErr. I’ll leave it as an exercise for the reader to write an additional test to get 100% test code coverage. Initial Code Coverage for DoMath Figure 6-1. Initial code coverage Final Code Coverage for DoMath Figure 6-2. Final code coverage Code coverage is a great thing, but it’s not enough. There’s actually a bug in your code, even though you have 100% coverage. Have you noticed it? If not, add another test case and rerun your tests: {"another_mult", 2, 3, "*", 6, nil}, You should see the error: table_test.go:60: Expected 6, got 5 Your case for multiplication has a typo. It adds the numbers together instead of multiplying them. (Beware the dangers of copy-and-paste coding!) Fix the code, rerun go test -v -cover -coverprofile=c.out and go tool cover -html=c.out, and you’ll see that the tests pass again. Warning Code coverage is necessary but not sufficient. You can have 100% code coverage and still have bugs in your code!

title: Choosing the Right for Statement
text: Choosing the Right for Statement Now that I’ve covered all forms of the for statement, you might be wondering when to use which format. Most of the time, you should use the for-range format. A for-range loop is the best way to iterate up to an integer. It’s also the best way to walk through a string, since it properly gives you back runes instead of bytes. You have also seen that a for-range loop works well for iterating through slices and maps. Functional iterators make map and slice iteration more flexible and extend the idiom to user-defined types. You’ll see in the related discussion that channels work naturally with for-range as well. Tip Favor the for-range loop. For common cases, it avoids a great deal of the boilerplate code required for the other for loop styles. When should you use the complete for loop? It’s most useful when there’s a nontrivial increment or test. While you might be able to use some combination of if, continue, and break within a for-range loop, a standard for loop’s test and increment clauses provide a clear way to indicate when iteration ends and how many elements are being skipped. For example, here’s code that counts the number of runes in a slice of bytes: b := []byte{0xf0, 0x9f, 0x91, 0x8b, 0x2c, 0x20, 0xf0, 0x9f, 0x8c, 0x8e, 0x21} count := 0 width := 0 for i := 0; i < len(b); i += width { _, width = utf8.DecodeRune(b[i:]) count++ } fmt.Println(count) The size of the increment depends on the value of the data, which cannot work with a simple for-range loop over a slice. The condition-only for loop is, like the while loop it replaces, useful when you are looping based on a calculated value. The infinite for loop is useful in some situations, but you need to use it carefully. The body of the for loop should always contain a break or return, because you’ll rarely want to loop forever. Real-world programs should bound iteration and fail gracefully when they can’t complete operations. As you’ve seen, an infinite for loop can be combined with an if statement to simulate the do statements present in other languages. An infinite for loop is used to implement some versions of the iterator pattern, which you will look at when I review the standard library in the related discussion. It’s also used in the for-select loop concurrency pattern, which is covered in the related discussion. The lifespan of a for-loop variable Variables declared in the body of a for loop are recreated on each iteration. What might be surprising is that the variables declared in the for loop’s initialization section are also recreated on each iteration. For example, when you write the following code, the loop creates a new variable named i 10 times: for i := range 10 { fmt.Println("I'm a new i:", i) } In most situations, this behavior is invisible; it looks like the same instance is being reused and assigned a new value. In versions of Go before 1.22, the initialization section variables were created once and reused on each iteration through the for loop. That behavior was changed because reusing the variables resulted in subtle bugs when they were referenced within closures declared in the for loop body. (I discuss closures in detail in “Closures”.) Even though this change eliminated a potential bug, it was a backward-breaking change. You can control whether to enable it by specifying the Go version in the go directive in the go.mod file for your module. I talk about this in greater detail in the related discussion.

title: Choosing with switch
text: Choosing with switch Like many C-derived languages, Go has a switch statement. Most developers in those languages avoid switch statements because of their limitations on values that can be switched on and the default fallthrough behavior. But Go is different: It makes switch statements useful. Note For those readers who are more familiar with Go, I’m going to cover expression switch statements in this topic. I’ll discuss type switch statements when I talk about interfaces in the related discussion. At first glance, switch statements in Go don’t look all that different from how they appear in C/C++, Java, or JavaScript, but there are a few surprises. Let’s take a look at a sample switch statement. You can run the code in Example 3-20 on The Go Playground. Example 3-20. The switch statement words := []string{"a", "cow", "smile", "gopher", "octopus", "anthropologist"} for _, word := range words { switch size := len(word); size { case 1, 2, 3, 4: fmt.Println(word, "is a short word!") case 5: wordLen := len(word) fmt.Println(word, "is exactly the right length:", wordLen) case 6, 7, 8, 9: default: fmt.Println(word, "is a long word!") } } When you run this code, you get the following output: a is a short word! cow is a short word! smile is exactly the right length: 5 anthropologist is a long word! I will go over the features of the switch statement to explain the output. As with if statements, you don’t put parentheses around the value being compared in a switch. Also, you can declare a variable that’s scoped to all branches of the switch statement. In this case, you are scoping the variable size to all cases in the switch statement. All case clauses (and the optional default clause) are contained inside a set of braces—​but don’t put braces around the contents of the case clauses. You can have multiple lines inside a case (or default) clause, and they are all considered part of the same block. Inside case 5:, declare wordLen, a new variable. Since this is a new block, you can declare new variables within it. Just like any other block, any variables declared within a case clause’s block are visible only within that block. If you’re used to putting a break statement at the end of every case in your switch statements, you’ll be happy to notice that they are gone. By default, cases in switch statements in Go don’t fall through. This is more in line with the behavior in Ruby or (if you are an old-school programmer) Pascal. This prompts the question: if cases don’t fall through, what do you do if there are multiple values that should trigger the exact same logic? In Go, you separate multiple matches with commas, as you do when matching 1, 2, 3, and 4 or 6, 7, 8, and 9. That’s why you get the same output for both a and cow. Which leads to the next question: If you don’t have fallthrough and you have an empty case (as you do in the sample program when the length of your argument is 6, 7, 8, or 9 characters), what happens? In Go, an empty case means nothing happens. That’s why you don’t see any output from your program when you use octopus or gopher as the parameter. Tip For the sake of completeness, Go does include a fallthrough keyword, which lets one case continue on to the next one. Please think twice before implementing an algorithm that uses it. If you find yourself needing to use fallthrough, try to restructure your logic to remove the dependencies between cases. In the sample program, you are switching on the value of an integer, but that’s not all you can do. You can switch on any type that can be compared with ==, which includes all built-in types except slices, maps, functions, structs that contain fields of these types, and arrays with noncomparable element types. Even though you don’t need to put a break statement at the end of each case clause, you can use them when you want to exit early from a case. However, the need for a break statement might indicate that you’re doing something too complicated. Consider refactoring your code to remove it. There’s one more place where you might find yourself using a break statement in a case in a switch statement: If you have a switch statement inside a for loop and you want to break out of the for loop, put a label on the for statement and put the name of the label on the break. If you don’t use a label, Go assumes that you want to break out of the case. Let’s look at a quick example, where you want to break out of the for loop once it reaches 7. You can run the code in Example 3-21 on The Go Playground. Example 3-21. The case of the missing label func main() { for i := range 10 { switch i { case 0, 2, 4, 6: fmt.Println(i, "is even") case 3: fmt.Println(i, "is divisible by 3 but not 2") case 7: fmt.Println("exit the loop!") break default: fmt.Println(i, "is boring") } } } Running this code produces the following output: 0 is even 1 is boring 2 is even 3 is divisible by 3 but not 2 4 is even 5 is boring 6 is even exit the loop! 8 is boring 9 is boring That’s not what was intended. The goal was for this code to break out of the for loop when it got a 7, but instead, it interpreted the break was as exiting the case. To resolve this, you need to introduce a label, just as you did when breaking out of a nested for loop. First, you label the for statement: loop: for i := range 10 { Then you use the label on your break: break loop You can see these changes on The Go Playground. When you run it again, you get the expected output: 0 is even 1 is boring 2 is even 3 is divisible by 3 but not 2 4 is even 5 is boring 6 is even exit the loop! Blank Switches You can use switch statements in another, more powerful way. Just as Go allows you to leave out parts from a for statement’s declaration, you can write a switch statement that doesn’t specify the value that you’re comparing against. This is called a blank switch. A regular switch only allows you to check a value for equality. A blank switch allows you to use any Boolean comparison for each case. You can try out the code in Example 3-22 on The Go Playground. Example 3-22. The blank switch words := []string{"hi", "salutations", "hello"} for _, word := range words { switch wordLen := len(word); { case wordLen < 5: fmt.Println(word, "is a short word!") case wordLen > 10: fmt.Println(word, "is a long word!") default: fmt.Println(word, "is exactly the right length.") } } When you run this program, you get the following output: hi is a short word! salutations is a long word! hello is exactly the right length. Just as with a regular switch statement, you can optionally include a short variable declaration as part of your blank switch. But unlike a regular switch, you can write logical tests for your cases. Blank switches are pretty cool, but don’t overdo them. You may you find that you have written a blank switch where all your cases are equality comparisons against the same variable: switch { case a == 2: fmt.Println("a is 2") case a == 3: fmt.Println("a is 3") case a == 4: fmt.Println("a is 4") default: fmt.Println("a is ", a) } If so, replace it with an expression switch statement: switch a { case 2: fmt.Println("a is 2") case 3: fmt.Println("a is 3") case 4: fmt.Println("a is 4") default: fmt.Println("a is ", a) } Choosing Between if and switch As a matter of functionality, there isn’t much difference between a series of if/else statements and a blank switch statement. Both allow a series of comparisons. So, when should you use switch, and when should you use a set of if or if/else statements? A switch statement, even a blank switch, indicates that a relationship exists between the values or comparisons in each case. To demonstrate the difference in clarity, rewrite the FizzBuzz program from Example 3-11 using a blank switch, as shown in Example 3-23. You can also find this code in the examples/simplest_fizzbuzz directory. Example 3-23. Rewriting a series of if statements with a blank switch for i := 1; i <= 100; i++ { switch { case i%3 == 0 && i%5 == 0: fmt.Println("FizzBuzz") case i%3 == 0: fmt.Println("Fizz") case i%5 == 0: fmt.Println("Buzz") default: fmt.Println(i) } } Most people would agree that this is the most readable version. There’s no more need for continue statements, and the default behavior is made explicit with the default case. Of course, nothing in Go prevents you from doing all sorts of unrelated comparisons on each case in a blank switch. However, this is not idiomatic. If you find that you want to do this, use a series of if/else statements instead (or perhaps consider refactoring your code). Tip Favor blank switch statements over if/else chains when you have multiple related cases. Using a switch makes the comparisons more visible and reinforces that they are a related set of concerns.

title: Cleaning up with defer
text: Cleaning up with defer Programs often create temporary resources, like files or network connections, that need to be cleaned up, no matter how many exit points the function has, or whether it completes successfully. In Go, the cleanup code is attached to the function with the defer keyword. Let’s take a look at how to use defer to release resources. You’ll do this by writing a simple version of cat, the Unix utility for printing the contents of a file. You can’t pass in arguments on the Go Playground, but you can find the code for this example in the examples/simple_cat directory. This example introduces a few new features that I’ll cover in more detail in later chapters: func main() { if len(os.Args) < 2 { slog.Error("no file specified") os.Exit(1) } os.Exit(run()) } func run() int { f, err := os.Open(os.Args[1]) if err != nil { slog.Error("open failed", slog.Any("err", err)) return 1 } defer f.Close() data := make([]byte, 2048) for { count, err := f.Read(data) os.Stdout.Write(data[:count]) if err != nil { if err != io.EOF { slog.Error("read failed", slog.Any("err", err)) return 1 } break } } return 0 } First, the program ensures that a filename is specified on the command line by checking the length of os.Args , a slice in the os package. The first value in os.Args is the program name. The remaining values are the arguments passed to the program. Check that the length of os.Args is at least 2 to determine whether the argument was provided to the program. If it wasn’t, the program will call the Error function in the log/slog package to print a message, and end execution using os.Exit (1) to indicate that it has exited due to an error. Next, the run function is called. In run, the program tries to acquire a read-only file handle via the Open function in the os package. The second value returned by Open is an error. If there’s a problem opening the file, it will print the error message and return 1. Once you know there is a valid file handle, you need to close it after you use it, no matter how you exit the function. To ensure that the cleanup code runs, use the defer keyword followed by a function or method call. In this case, you’ll use the Close method on the file variable. Normally, a function call would run immediately, but defer delays its invocation until the surrounding function exits. You can read from a file handle by passing a slice of bytes to the Read method on a file variable. I’ll cover how to use this method in detail in the related discussion, but for now, know that Read returns the number of bytes that were read into the slice, along with an error. If an error occurs, check whether it’s an end-of-file marker. If you’re at the end of the file, use break to exit the for loop. Report all other errors using slog.Error and exit run with a value of 1. I’ll talk a little more about slices and function parameters in “Go Is Call by Value” and will go into more detail on this pattern when I discuss pointers in this topic. If the file is read to the end, run returns 0. Finally, the flow of execution returns to main, and the value returned from run is passed to os.Exit . A 0 indicates the program has exited normally; a 1 indicates that an error has occurred. Building and running the program from within the simple_cat directory produces the following result: $ go build $ ./simple_cat main.go package main import ( "io" "log/slog" "os" ) ... Tip Why is most of this program outside of main? It’s because of defer. By convention, a program that exits due to an error returns a nonzero exit code. In Go, you indicate this with the os.Exit function. The problem is that calling os.Exit immediately exits the program, which means that any deferred functions are skipped. To ensure that deferred functions run, only call os.Exit from main, and do not use defer in main if there’s an os.Exit . If you move most of the logic to run, the program can use defer to close resources properly and return the correct exit code on error. You should know a few more things about defer. First, you can use a function, method, or closure with defer. (When I mention functions with defer, you can mentally expand that to “functions, methods, or closures.”) You can defer multiple functions in a Go function. They run in last-in, first-out (LIFO) order; the last defer registered runs first. The code within defer functions runs after the return statement. As I mentioned, you can supply a function with input parameters to a defer. The input parameters are evaluated immediately and their values are stored until the function runs. Here’s a quick example that demonstrates both of these features of defer: func deferExample() int { a := 10 defer func(val int) { fmt.Println("first:", val) }(a) a = 20 defer func(val int) { fmt.Println("second:", val) }(a) a = 30 fmt.Println("exiting:", a) return a } Running this code gives the following output: exiting: 30 second: 20 first: 10 You can run this on The Go Playground. It is also available in the examples/defer_example directory. Note You can supply a function that returns values to a defer, but there’s no way to read those values: func example() { defer func() int { return 2 // there's no way to read this value }() } You might be wondering whether there’s a way for a deferred function to examine or modify the return values of its surrounding function. There is, and it’s the best reason to use named return values. It allows your code to take actions based on an error. When I talk about errors in the related discussion>, I will discuss a pattern that uses defer to add contextual information to an error returned from a function. Let’s look at a way to clean up database transactions using named return values and defer: func DoSomeInserts(ctx context.Context, db *sql.DB, value1, value2 string) (err error) { tx, err := db.BeginTx(ctx, nil) if err != nil { return err } defer func() { if err == nil { err = tx.Commit() } if err != nil { tx.Rollback() } }() _, err = tx.ExecContext(ctx, "INSERT INTO FOO (val) values $1", value1) if err != nil { return err } // use tx to do more database inserts here with value2 return nil } I’m not going to cover Go’s database support in these notes, but the standard library includes extensive support for databases in the database/sql package. In the example function, you create a transaction to do a series of database inserts. If any of them fails, roll back rather than modifying the database. If they all succeed, commit (store the database changes). Use a closure with defer to check whether err has been assigned a value. If it hasn’t, run tx.Commit . This could also return an error. If it does, the value err is modified. If any database interaction returns an error, call tx.Rollback . Note New Go developers tend to forget the set of parentheses that goes after the braces when specifying a function for defer. It is a compile-time error to leave them out, so eventually the habit sets in. It helps to remember that supplying parentheses allows you to specify values that will be passed into the function when it runs. Another common pattern in Go: a function that allocates a resource can also return a closure that cleans up the resource. In the examples/simple_cat_cancel directory, there is a rewrite of the simple cat program that does this. First you write a helper function that opens a file and returns a closure: func openFile(name string) (*os.File, func(), error) { file, err := os.Open(name) if err != nil { return nil, nil, err } return file, func() { file.Close() }, nil } The helper function returns a file, a function, and an error. That * means that a file reference in Go is a pointer. I’ll talk more about that in this topic. Now, in run, use the openFile function: f, closer, err := openFile(os.Args[1]) if err != nil { slog.Error("cannot open file", slog.Any("err", err)) return 1 } defer closer() Because Go doesn’t allow unused variables, returning the closer from the function means that the program will not compile if the function isn’t called. That reminds the user to use defer. As covered earlier, put parentheses after closer when you defer it. Note Using defer can feel strange if you are used to a language that uses a block within a function to control resource cleanup, like the try/catch/finally blocks in Java, JavaScript, and Python or the begin/rescue/ensure blocks in Ruby. The downside to these resource-cleanup blocks is that they create another level of indentation in your function, which makes the code harder to read. It’s not just my opinion that nested code is harder to follow: In research described in a 2017 paper in Empirical Software Engineering, Vard Antinyan et al. discovered that “Of …​ eleven proposed code characteristics, only two markedly influence complexity growth: the nesting depth and the lack of structure.” There is a wide body of research on what makes a program easier to read and understand. You can find papers many decades old, including a 1983 paper by Richard Miara et al. that tries to figure out the right amount of indentation to use (according to their results, two to four spaces).

title: Cleanup, Context, and Helper
text: Cleanup, Context, and Helper The Cleanup method on * testing.T is used to clean up temporary resources created for a single test. This method has a single parameter: a function with no input parameters or return values. The function runs when the test completes. For simple tests, you can achieve the same result by using a defer statement, but Cleanup is useful when tests rely on helper functions to set up sample data. It’s fine to call Cleanup multiple times. Just like defer, the functions are invoked in last-added, first-called order. Example 6-1 demonstrates a test helper function that uses Cleanup: Example 6-1. A Test Helper with t.Cleanup and t.Helper func TestAddressQuery(t *testing.T) { db := setupDB(t, "address") address, err := FindAddress(t.Context(), db, "Fred") if err != nil { t.Error(err) } if address.Country != "Australia" { t.Error("wrong country") } } func setupDB(t *testing.T, tableName string) *sql.DB { t.Helper() db, err := sql.Open("ramsql", tableName) if err != nil { t.Fatal("error creating database", err) } t.Cleanup(func() { db.Close() }) return db } Functions like setupDB are referred to as test helpers since they set up or tear down the state needed to properly test code, but do no testing themselves. If something goes wrong it is usually a fatal error, as the test cannot continue without valid initial conditions. To mark the function as a test helper, it is idiomatic to pass a * testing.T instance to these functions and add a call to t.Helper as the first line. When t.Helper is called, it modifies the output of any calls to t.Error or t.Fatal within the test helper. Rather than print the filename and line number of the line in the test helper, the filename and line number of the line in the test function that called the test helper is displayed. This is useful when a helper function is called from multiple tests; you’ll see the name of the test and the line where the helper was called in the error output. In this example, the helper function setupDB creates a per-test database connection. Inside of setupDB, Cleanup is called to close the database connection when the test exits. We can’t use a defer here, because defer runs when a function exits and we want to close the connection when the test ends. Another thing to notice is in TestAddressQuery. The context that’s passed into FindAddress comes from the t.Context method. This is a special context that is automatically canceled when the test exits. Using it allows any code being tested to shut down properly when the test ends. Prefer using t.Context in tests over context.Background . You can find this sample code in the examples/helper directory has an example. It is also available on the Go Playground. Change "ramsql" to some other string and run the test with the t.Helper () line commented and then uncommented to see the difference it makes in the error output.

title: Closures
text: Closures Functions declared inside functions are special; they are called closures. This is a computer-science word that means that functions declared inside functions can access and modify variables declared in the outer function. Let’s look at a quick example to see how this works. You can find the code on The Go Playground. The code is also in the examples/closure directory: func main() { a := 20 f := func() { fmt.Println(a) a = 30 } f() fmt.Println(a) } Running this program gives the following output: 20 30 The anonymous function assigned to f can read and write a, even though a is not passed into it. Just as with any inner scope, you can shadow a variable inside a closure. Try changing the code to: func main() { a := 20 f := func() { fmt.Println(a) a := 30 fmt.Println(a) } f() fmt.Println(a) } This will print out the following: 20 30 20 Using := instead of = inside the closure creates a new a that ceases to exist when the closure exits. When working with inner functions, be careful to use the correct assignment operator, especially when multiple variables are on the left-hand side. You can try this code on The Go Playground. The code is also in the examples/closure_shadow directory. This inner function and closure stuff might not seem all that useful at first. What benefit do you get from making mini-functions within a larger function? Why does Go have this feature? One thing that closures allow you to do is to limit a function’s scope. If a function is going to be called from only one other function, but it’s called multiple times, you can use an inner function to “hide” the called function. This reduces the number of declarations at the package level, which can make it easier to find an unused name. If you have a piece of logic that is repeated multiple times within a function, you can use a closure to remove that repetition. For example, a simple Lisp interpreter can use a Scan function that processes an input string to find the parts of a Lisp program. It relies on two closures, buildCurToken and update, to make the code shorter and easier to understand. Closures really become interesting when they are passed to other functions or returned from a function. They allow you to take the variables within your function and use them outside of your function. Passing Functions as Parameters Since functions are values and you can specify function’s type using its parameter and return types, you can pass functions as parameters into functions. If you aren’t used to treating functions like data, take a moment to think about the implications of creating a closure that references local variables and then passing that closure to another function. It’s a very useful pattern that appears several times in the standard library. The slices and maps packages have many functions with function parameters. In “Comparing Slices” and “Comparing Maps”, you learned about slices.EqualFunc and maps.EqualFunc , which use a function parameter to test equality for elements in the containers. Another example is sorting slices. The slices package in the standard library has a function called slices.Sort that takes in a slice and sorts the values in it. However, it only works for slices whose elements are of an ordered type, and it only sorts thw values in ascending order. (As a reminder, an ordered type is one that can be compared with >, <, >=, and ⇐.) If you want to sort a slice that contains elements of a nonordered type, or if you want to specify your own sort order, use the slices.SortFunc function. Let’s see how it works by sorting a slice of a struct with multiple fields. Here’s the sample data: type Person struct { FirstName string LastName string Age int } people := []Person{ {"Pat", "Patterson", 37}, {"Tracy", "Bobdaughter", 23}, {"Fred", "Fredson", 18}, {"Fred", "Fredson", 92}, {"Mary", "Patterson", 42}, } You can’t use slices.Sort to sort this slice, because Person isn’t an ordered type. Here is the code to sort this slice by last name in ascending alphabetical order: slices.SortFunc(people, func(p1, p2 Person) int { switch { case p1.LastName < p2.LastName: return -1 case p1.LastName > p2.LastName: return 1 default: return 0 } }) Note The people slice is changed by the call to slices.SortFunc . I talk about this briefly in “Go Is Call by Value” and in more detail in this topic. SortFunc takes in a slice and a compare function. A compare function takes in two parameters of the same type and returns an int. It returns a value less than 0 when the first parameter is ordered before the second parameter, 0 when the parameters are considered identical, and greater than 0 when the second parameter is ordered before the first parameter. If you are building a comparison function out of orderable types, the Go standard library contains a useful helper function. While Person isn’t orderable, its LastName field is. Call the cmp.Compare function with the fields you are comparing to remove a lot of ugly boilerplate code: slices.SortFunc(people, func(p1, p2 Person) int { return cmp.Compare(p1.LastName, p2.LastName) }) Here are few more sorting variations. To sort by last name, descending, swap the order of the parameters to cmp.Compare : slices.SortFunc(people, func(p1, p2 Person) int { return cmp.Compare(p2.LastName, p1.LastName) }) What if you want to sort by multiple fields? The cmp package includes another useful function called Or. It takes in zero or more values and returns the first nonzero value. If all of the values are 0, cmp.Or returns 0. Combining cmp.Or with cmp.Compare allows you to list multiple compare functions. The first nonzero value determines the order of the two values. If all of the compare functions return 0, the values are equal. Here is how to use it to sort by last name, first name, and age: slices.SortFunc(people, func(p1, p2 Person) int { return cmp.Or( cmp.Compare(p1.LastName, p2.LastName), cmp.Compare(p1.FirstName, p2.FirstName), cmp.Compare(p1.Age, p2.Age), ) }) What if you want a configurable sort function? You can take advantage of closures’ ability to capture a local variable (which is the official computer-science way to say that closures can access local variables) and pass a function to slices.SortFunc that reads the value of function parameters to determine how to sort them: func PeopleSorter(people []Person, sortBy string, direction string) { slices.SortFunc(people, func(p1, p2 Person) int { var out int switch sortBy { case "lastname": out = cmp.Compare(p1.LastName, p2.LastName) case "firstname": out = cmp.Compare(p1.FirstName, p2.FirstName) case "age": out = cmp.Compare(p1.Age, p2.Age) default: out = 0 // don't sort } if direction == "desc" { out = -out } return out }) } Tip Passing functions as parameters to other functions is often useful for performing different operations on the same kind of data. You can try out this code on the Go Playground. One common pattern in the standard library is pairing Sort with SortFunc: a function that provides a standard behavior for a specific set of types, and a Func variant that has a function parameter to support additional types and implement customized behavior. You’ve already seen slices.Equal with slices.EqualFunc and slices.Compare with slices.CompareFunc . There are more of these pairs in the slices package, including Contains/ContainsFunc, Delete/DeleteFunc, and Min/MinFunc. Note All of the functions I’ve used in these examples ( slices.Sort , slices.SortFunc , cmp.Compare , and cmp.Or ) take advantage of Go’s generics support. I’ll cover generics in detail in the related discussion. Returning Functions from Functions In addition to using a closure to pass some function state to another function, you can also return a closure from a function. Let’s demonstrate this by writing a function that returns a multiplier function. You can run this program on The Go Playground. The code is also in the examples/makeMult directory. Here is a function that returns a closure: func makeMult(base int) func(int) int { return func(factor int) int { return base * factor } } And here is how the function is used: func main() { twoBase := makeMult(2) threeBase := makeMult(3) for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { fmt.Println(twoBase(i), threeBase(i)) } } Running this program gives the following output: 0 0 2 3 4 6 Now that you’ve seen closures in action, you might wonder how often Go developers use them. As it turns out, they’re surprisingly useful. The slices and maps packages are mostly composed of functions that take in functions or return functions. The slices.Values function and the other functions I covered in “Iterating over functions” aren’t iterator functions themselves; they return closures that implement the iterator function types. You will see this pattern when you build middleware for a web server in the related discussion. Go also uses closures to implement resource cleanup, via the defer keyword. Note If you spend any time with programmers who use functional programming languages like Haskell, you might hear the term higher-order functions. That’s a fancy way to say that a function has a function for an input parameter or a return value. As a Go developer, you are as cool as they are!

title: Code Review: Advanced Testing
text: Code Review: Advanced Testing Code coverage is necessary, but not sufficient. Even code with 100% code coverage can contain bugs. Make sure that tests include multiple sets of data for the same paths through the code. And always test inputs that should produce errors. If your program processes data you don’t control (and most programs do), include fuzzing tests in your test suites. Don’t guess that your changes made the code faster---measure. Capture benchmarks and use Benchstat to track improvements and regressions over time. When testing concurrent code, use the data race detector to ensure you aren’t accessing shared data without locks and use synctest to make the tests fast and accurate.

title: Code Review: Basic Testing
text: Code Review: Basic Testing Take advantage of Go’s built-in testing framework to write idiomatic tests. Make sure that tests cover positive and negative cases. Use the testdata directory to hold data for running your tests. Use t.Context () instead of context.Background (). Consider whether go-cmp would simplify comparisons. Use table tests to validate the same logic with different data. If your tests are independent (and they should be), use t.Parallel ().

title: Code Review: Blocks, shadowing, and if statements
text: Code Review: Blocks, shadowing, and if statements Watch for accidental shadowing when using := in inner scopes. Do not give a local variable the same name as an imported package; this makes the package unreachable for the remainder of the enclosing block. Never redefine an identifier from the universe block. The compiler may not catch it, and the resulting bugs are subtle. If the variable being tested in the condition of an if statement is only useful within the if and else blocks, assign its value in the initialization section of the if statement so it is scoped to just the if and else blocks.

title: Code Review: Function values and closures
text: Code Review: Function values and closures If multiple functions with the same signature are used for similar purposes and assigned to variables, define a function type and use it when declaring the function variables. This clarifies the relationship between the functions and documents their purpose. Take care when using package-level function variables. Unlike function declarations, they are mutable, which means their functionality can be changed at runtime. If you have a helper function that’s only used within a single function, consider using a closure for the helper function. Use function parameters to “plug in” logic to a larger algorithm, such as to specify the sort order when sorting a slice. Default to using cmp.Compare and cmp.Or when writing comparator functions.

title: Code Review: Intro to pointers, new, and shallow copies
text: Code Review: Intro to pointers, new, and shallow copies Structs and primitive types in Go can be either pointers or values. In many other languages, primitive types are always values and classes are always pointers. Use new to make a pointer out of a constant or literal value, or to make a non-nil pointer to an instance of a type. When a variable is passed to new, it makes a pointer to a shallow copy of the variable. Pointer fields in the copy still alias the original’s data. Use & when you mean to reference the original, not duplicate it.

title: Code Review: Slices and Arrays
text: Code Review: Slices and Arrays Use slices instead of arrays, unless the number of elements never changes. Prefer nil slices to empty slice literals. If you know how many elements you need in a slice, size it with make. Don’t use make([]T, length) to create a slice and then append the slice. append adds new values to the end of a slice, starting at position length+1. Use slices.Clone (or copy with a sized destination) to duplicate a slice. Be very careful when slicing slices. Treat the resulting slices as read-only to avoid data sharing surprises. Before writing your own slice manipulation function, check the standard library to make sure it hasn’t already been implemented.

title: Code Review: Strings and Maps
text: Code Review: Strings and Maps Don’t slice or index a string unless you know it’s single-byte content. Never convert an int to string with string(x). Always initialize maps before writing. Use the comma-ok idiom whenever a map’s zero value is a legitimate value. Check the slices, bytes, and maps packages before writing your own helper.

title: Code Review: Structs
text: Code Review: Structs Use structs to group related data. Use named struct literals for anything beyond two or three fields. Use a struct, not a map, when you have a known set of fields. Don’t fight against the type system.

title: Code Review: Tests with Mocks and Stubs
text: Code Review: Tests with Mocks and Stubs Make sure your code interacts with other components via abstractions. They make code easier to understand and easier to test. Prefer function-field stubs over switch-statement stubs when the same method needs different behavior across test cases. Stubs are useful for testing, but verify that usign one is helping you test your production code, not the stub itself. Use httptest to validate that the HTTP clients in your code are both sending and receiving data correctly. Separate unit tests from integration test via tags or environment variables.

title: Code Review: Using Pointers, Slices, and Maps
text: Code Review: Using Pointers, Slices, and Maps Prefer value parameters. Use a pointer parameter only when the function must mutate the caller’s value, the type must not be copied, or a struct is genuinely large. If you must optimize performance, always measure before switching to a pointer return value. For small data, returning a value is usually faster. Maps make bad parameters and return values—​not only because they aren’t self-documenting, but because they are always mutable. Prefer a struct unless you don’t know the keys at compile time. Document when a function modifies the contents of a slice argument.

title: Code Review: Working with the Garbage Collector
text: Code Review: Working with the Garbage Collector Try to lay out your data structures sequentially in memory, so they can be loaded from RAM efficiently. Always check to see if a weak pointer’s Value() method returns nil before using the value; the garbage collector may have collected the wrapped pointer. If you know exactly how big a slice needs to be, allocate it with a constant so the compiler can store it on the stack. Check the garbage-collector stats if your code is running slower than expected. If other techniques fail, use the GOMEMLIMIT and GOGC variables to fine-tune your application’s memory usage.

title: Code Review: defer and call by value
text: Code Review: defer and call by value Use defer to make sure that resources are cleaned up when a function exits. For functions that allocate a resource, consider returning a cleanup closure. The unused-variable rule reminds the caller to defer it. Use named return values if a deferred function can modify a function’s return value. Keep your functions shallow; don’t nest the indentations too deeply. Using defer and early returns helps avoid the deep indentation of try/finally-style cleanups. Unlike primitive values and structs, map and slice parameters can be mutated. Use comments on your functions to document when your function mutates the values of its parameters so users of the function know that passed-in values aren’t read-only.

title: Code Review: for loops
text: Code Review: for loops Prefer for-range loops, especially when you’re iterating over every element in a compound type. They are also the easiest way to walk a string by runes or count up to a specified integer. Go forbids unused declared variables, including loop variables. If you don’t need the first iteration variable in a range expression that returns two iteration variables, use the blank identifier _. Never rely on map iteration order. It varies between runs by design. Use range over function for alternate ways to iterate over slices, maps, and strings, or to iterate through user-defined container types. Avoid deeply indented blocks. If possible, use break and continue to avoid deeply nested code within for loops. Use labels with break or continue to exit or advance iteration of an outer loop when inside a nested one. Never write a infinite for loop in production code. There must be some condition in the body that reaches a break or return. Real programs bound iteration and fail gracefully.

title: Code Review: functions, parameters, and return values
text: Code Review: functions, parameters, and return values A function shouldn’t have a lot of parameters. Make sure your function isn’t doing too much. Outside of fmt.Println and other well-known functions, use _ to explicitly mark ignored return values. Never use a blank (naked) return in a function that returns values. It forces the reader to scan the entire function to figure out what value is being returned. Watch out for shadowing named return values. Confirm that you’re assigning to the return variable, not accidentally creating a new one with := .

title: Code Review: switch and goto
text: Code Review: switch and goto A break keyword only breaks out of its immediate scope. If you have a switch statement inside a for loop, a break in one of the switch statement’s case clauses breaks out of the case, not the for loop. Use a labeled break if you want to exit the for loop from a case. Prefer a blank switch over a series of if and else blocks when the cases are related comparisons. The switch signals the relationship, aligns the conditions, and makes the default explicit. Avoid fallthrough. While it can be helpful in rare cases, reconsider your implementation if you find yourself using it. Use goto only when the alternatives, like Boolean flags or code duplication, make the code’s logic harder to understand.

title: Comparing Maps
text: Comparing Maps Go 1.21 added a package to the standard library called maps that contains helper functions for working with maps. Two functions in the package are useful for comparing if two maps are equal, maps.Equal and maps.EqualFunc . They are analogous to the slices.Equal and slices.EqualFunc functions. Use maps.Equal when the values in the map are comparable (as previously mentioned, the keys in a map are required to be comparable): m := map[string]int{ "hello": 5, "world": 10, } n := map[string]int{ "world": 10, "hello": 5, } fmt.Println(maps.Equal(m, n)) // prints true If the values are not comparable, use maps.EqualFunc to provide a function that determines equality. Try out this example on The Go Playground: m := map[string][]int{ "team_a": []int{8, 6, 7}, "team_b": []int{5, 3, 0, 9}, } n := map[string][]int{ "team_a": []int{8, 6, 7}, "team_b": []int{5, 3, 0, 9}, } fmt.Println(maps.EqualFunc(m, n, slices.Equal)) // prints true If you want a different definition of equality than what Go provides by default, you can use maps.EqualFunc (or slices.EqualFunc ) with a comparable type. For example, you could implement a case-insensitive comparison of map values. Try it out on The Go Playground: m := map[int]string{ 10: "hello", 20: "goodbye", 30: "peace", } n := map[int]string{ 10: "HELLO", 20: "GOODBYE", 30: "PEACE", } fmt.Println(maps.EqualFunc(m, n, strings.EqualFold)) // prints true

title: Comparing Slices
text: Comparing Slices As I mentioned earlier, slices are not comparable, which means they cannot be compared to each other using the == and != operators (slices can only be compared to nil ). If you need to test if two slices have identical sizes and contents, the slices package in the standard library provides two functions. The slices.Equal function takes in two slices and returns true if the slices are the same length, and all of the elements are equal. It requires the elements of the slice to be comparable. The other function, slices.EqualFunc , lets you pass in a function to determine equality and does not require the slice elements to be comparable. You’ll learn about passing functions into functions in “Passing Functions as Parameters”. You can see how Equal and EqualFunc are used on the Go Playground: x := []int{1, 2, 3} y := []int{4, 5, 6} z := []int{1, 2, 3} fmt.Println(slices.Equal(x, y)) // prints false fmt.Println(slices.Equal(x, z)) // prints true a := [][]int{{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}} b := [][]int{{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}} // pass slices.Equal in to slices.EqualFunc to // compare elements that are slices of comparable values fmt.Println(slices.EqualFunc(a, b, slices.Equal)) // prints true Slices are also not an ordered type. That means you cannot use them with the <, <=, >, and >= operators. Just like equality testing, the slices package provides two functions to determine if one slice is greater than, equal to, or less than another slice. The first is Compare and is only usable if the elements of the slice are an ordered type (only integers types, floating point types, and string are ordered types). Compare returns -1 if the first slice is “less than” the second slice, 1 if the first slice is “greater than” the second slice, and 0 if the slices are identical. If the elements are not an ordered type, use the CompareFunc function, passing in the slices and a function that compares an element of the slice. You can see how Compare and CompareFunc are used on the Go Playground: x := []int{1, 2, 3} y := []int{4, 5, 6} z := []int{1, 2, 3} fmt.Println(slices.Compare(x, y)) // prints -1 fmt.Println(slices.Compare(x, z)) // prints 0 a := [][]int{{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}} b := [][]int{{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}} // pass slices.Compare in to slices.CompareFunc to // compare elements that are slices of ordered values fmt.Println(slices.CompareFunc(a, b, slices.Compare)) // prints 0 Warning The reflect package contains a function called DeepEqual that can compare almost anything, including slices. It’s a legacy function, primarily intended for testing. Before the inclusion of slices.Equal and slices.EqualFunc , reflect.DeepEqual was often used to compare slices. Don’t use it in new code, as it is slower and less safe than using the functions in the slices package.

title: Converting Arrays to Slices
text: Converting Arrays to Slices Slices aren’t the only thing you can slice. If you have an array, you can take a slice from it using a slice expression. This is a useful way to bridge an array to a function that takes only slices. To convert an entire array into a slice, use the [:] syntax: xArray := [4]int{5, 6, 7, 8} xSlice := xArray[:] You can also convert a subset of an array into a slice: x := [4]int{5, 6, 7, 8} y := x[:2] z := x[2:] Be aware that taking a slice from an array has the same memory-sharing properties as taking a slice from a slice. If you run the following code on The Go Playground: x := [4]int{5, 6, 7, 8} y := x[:2] z := x[2:] x[0] = 10 fmt.Println("x:", x) fmt.Println("y:", y) fmt.Println("z:", z) you get this output: x: [10 6 7 8] y: [10 6] z: [7 8] You can use copy with arrays by taking a slice of the array. You can make the array either the source or the destination of the copy. You can try out the following code on The Go Playground: x := []int{1, 2, 3, 4} d := [4]int{5, 6, 7, 8} y := make([]int, 2) copy(y, d[:]) fmt.Println(y) copy(d[:], x) fmt.Println(d) The first call to copy copies the first two values in array d into slice y. The second copies all of the values in slice x into array d. This produces the following output: [5 6] [1 2 3 4]

title: Converting Slices to Arrays
text: Converting Slices to Arrays Use a type conversion to make an array variable from a slice. You can convert an entire slice to an array of the same type, or you can create an array from a subset of the slice. When you convert a slice to an array, the data in the slice is copied to new memory. That means that changes to the slice won’t affect the array, and vice versa. The following code: xSlice := []int{1, 2, 3, 4} xArray := [4]int(xSlice) smallArray := [2]int(xSlice) xSlice[0] = 10 fmt.Println(xSlice) fmt.Println(xArray) fmt.Println(smallArray) prints out: [10 2 3 4] [1 2 3 4] [1 2] The size of the array must be specified at compile time. It’s a compile-time error to use [...] in a slice to array type conversion. While the size of the array can be smaller than the size of the slice, it cannot be bigger. Unfortunately, the compiler cannot detect this, and your code will panic at runtime if you specify an array size that’s bigger than the length (not the capacity) of the slice. The following code: panicArray := [5]int(xSlice) fmt.Println(panicArray) panics at runtime with the message: panic: runtime error: cannot convert slice with length 4 to array or pointer to array with length 5 Note I haven’t talked about pointers yet, but you can also use a type conversion to convert a slice into a pointer to an array: xSlice := []int{1,2,3,4} xArrayPointer := (*[4]int)(xSlice) After converting a slice to an array pointer, the storage between the two is shared. A change to one will change the other: xSlice[0] = 10 xArrayPointer[1] = 20 fmt.Println(xSlice) // prints [10 20 3 4] fmt.Println(xArrayPointer) // prints &[10 20 3 4] Pointers are covered in the related discussion. You can try all of the array type conversions on The Go Playground. In “Arrays—Too Rigid to Use Directly”, I mentioned that you can’t use arrays as function parameters when the size of the array being passed in might vary. Technically, you can work around this limitation by converting an array to a slice, converting the slice to an array of a different size, and then passing the second array in to a function. The second array must be shorter than the first array, or your program will panic. While this might be helpful in a pinch, if you find yourself doing this frequently, strongly consider changing your function’s API to take a slice instead of an array.

title: Copying Maps
text: Copying Maps Assigning a map variable to another map variable shares the map between the two variables. If you modify one variable, the other is modified as well. This is similar to the way slices behave, which was discussed in “Sharing and Copying Slices”. Here is an example on The Go Playground: x := map[string]int{ "magic": 3, "hero": 0, "good": 11, } y := x y["naughty"] = 9 fmt.Println(x) // prints map[good:11 hero:0 magic:3 naughty:9] Like slices, Go provides two ways to duplicate a map. While the built-in function copy does not work for maps, the maps package provides a pair of methods for copying maps: Copy, which is similar to the built-in copy function for slices, and Clone, which is similar to slices.Clone . For maps.Copy , you pass in a destination map and a source map. All the key/value pairs in the source are copied to the destination. The destination map does not need to be empty; if it contains a key that is also in the source map, the value in the destination map is overwritten. You can see this behavior on The Go Playground: from := map[string]int{ "hello": 5, "world": 10, } to := map[string]int{ "hello": 30, "goodbye": 11, } maps.Copy(to, from) fmt.Println(to) // prints map[goodbye:11 hello:5 world:10] The maps.Clone function returns a new map with a copy of all the key/value pairs in the source map. You can see this on The Go Playground: x := map[string]int{ "uno": 1, "dos": 2, "tres": 3, } y := maps.Clone(x) y["catorce"] = 14 y["uno"] = 0 fmt.Println(x) // prints map[dos:2 tres:3 uno:1] fmt.Println(y) // prints map[catorce:14 dos:2 tres:3 uno:0] Notice that modifying the clone doesn’t modify the original. However, you should be aware of an interaction between pointers and the copy functions for maps and slices. These functions make shallow copies. When copying a value that contains a pointer, the data pointed to by the pointer isn’t duplicated; the pointer is. If the value pointed to by the pointer is modified, the modification appears in both the original and the copy. This is similar to the behavior you saw when assigning a map or slice to a new variable. You can see it demonstrated on The Go Playground: original := map[string][]int{ "fives": []int{0, 5, 10}, "threes": []int{0, 3, 6, 9}, } clone := maps.Clone(original) clone["fives"][0] = -5 clone["sixes"] = []int{0, 6, 12} fmt.Println(original["fives"], clone["fives"]) // prints [-5 5 10] [-5 5 10] fmt.Println(original["sixes"], clone["sixes"]) // prints [], [0 6 12] Both slices and maps contain pointers, which is why we see this behavior. Notice that adding a new entry to the clone doesn’t modify the original. It’s when you modify one of the slices that is already there that the change is shared. Again, I’ll cover pointers in detail in the related discussion.

title: Copying Slices of Slices
text: Copying Slices of Slices Slice expressions allow you to copy from the middle of the source slice: x := []int{1, 2, 3, 4} y := make([]int, 2) copy(y, x[2:]) You are copying the third and fourth elements in x by taking a slice of the slice. Also note that you don’t assign the output of copy to a variable. If you don’t need the number of elements copied, you don’t need to assign it. Combining the copy function with slice expressions allows you to do some unusual things, like copy between two slices that cover overlapping sections of an underlying slice: x := []int{1, 2, 3, 4} num := copy(x[:3], x[1:]) fmt.Println(x, num) In this case, you are copying the last three values in x on top of the first three values of x. This prints out [2 3 4 4] 3.

title: Declaring Your Slice
text: Declaring Your Slice Now that you’ve seen all these ways to create slices, how do you choose which slice declaration style to use? The primary goal is to minimize the number of times the slice needs to grow. If it’s possible that the slice won’t need to grow at all, use a var declaration with no assigned value to create a nil slice, as shown in Example 2-2. Example 2-2. Declaring a slice that might stay nil var data []int Note You can create a slice using an empty slice literal: var x = []int{} This creates a slice with zero length and zero capacity. It is confusingly different from a nil slice. Because of implementation reasons, comparing a zero-length slice to nil returns false, while comparing a nil slice to nil returns true. For simplicity, favor nil slices. If you have some starting values, or if a slice’s values aren’t going to change, then a slice literal is a good choice (see Example 2-3). Example 2-3. Declaring a slice with default values data := []int{2, 4, 6, 8} // numbers we appreciate If you have a good idea of how large your slice needs to be, but don’t know what those values will be when you are writing the program, use make. The question then becomes whether you should specify a nonzero length in the call to make or specify a zero length and a nonzero capacity. There are three possibilities: If you are using a slice as a buffer, then specify a nonzero length. If you are sure you know the exact size you want, you can specify the length and index into the slice to set the values. This is often done when transforming values in one slice and storing them in a second. The downside to this approach is that if you have the size wrong, you’ll end up with either zero values at the end of the slice or a panic from trying to access elements that don’t exist. In other situations, use make with a zero length and a specified capacity. This allows you to use append to add items to the slice. If the number of items turns out to be smaller, you won’t have an extraneous zero value at the end. If the number of items is larger, your code will not panic. The Go community is split between the second and third approaches. I personally prefer using append with a slice initialized to a zero length. It might be slower in some situations, but it is less likely to introduce a bug. Warning append always increases the length of a slice! If you have specified a slice’s length using make, be sure that you mean to append to it before you do so, or you might end up with a bunch of surprise zero values at the beginning of your slice.

title: Declaring and Calling Functions
text: Declaring and Calling Functions The basics of Go functions are familiar to anyone who has programmed in other languages with first-class functions, like C, Python, Ruby, or JavaScript. Just as with control structures, Go adds its own twist on function features. Some are improvements, and others are experiments that should be avoided. I’ll cover both in this topic. You’ve already seen functions being declared and used. Every Go program starts from a main function, and you’ve been calling the fmt.Println function to print to the screen. Since a main function doesn’t take in parameters or return values, let’s see what it looks like when a function does: func div(num int, denom int) int { if denom == 0 { return 0 } return num / denom } Let’s look at all the new things in this code sample. A function declaration has four parts: the keyword func, the name of the function, the input parameters, and the return type. The input parameters are listed in parentheses, separated by commas, with the parameter name first and the type second. Go is a typed language, so you must specify the types of the parameters. The return type is written between the input parameter’s closing parenthesis and the opening brace for the function body. Just like other languages, Go has a return keyword for returning values from a function. If a function returns a value, you must supply a return. If a function returns nothing, a return statement is not needed at the end, unless you are exiting from the function before the last line. The main function has no input parameters or return values. When a function has no input parameters, use empty parentheses (()). When a function returns nothing, you write nothing between the input parameter’s closing parenthesis and the opening brace for the function body: func main() { result := div(5, 2) fmt.Println(result) } The code for this simple program is in the examples/simple_div directory. Calling a function should be familiar to you as an experienced developer. On the right side of the := , you call the div function with the values 5 and 2. On the left side, you assign the returned value to the variable result. Tip When you have two or more consecutive input parameters of the same type, you can specify the type once for all of them like this: func div(num, denom int) int {

title: Deleting from Maps
text: Deleting from Maps Key-value pairs are removed from a map via the built-in delete function: m := map[string]int{ "hello": 5, "world": 10, } delete(m, "hello") The delete function takes a map and a key and then removes the key-value pair with the specified key. If the key isn’t present in the map or if the map is nil , nothing happens. The delete function doesn’t return a value.

title: Don’t Fear the Pointers
text: Don’t Fear the Pointers The first rule of pointers is: Don’t be afraid of pointers. If you are used to Java, JavaScript, Python, or Ruby, you might find them intimidating, but pointers are actually the familiar behavior for classes. It’s the nonpointer structs in Go that are unusual. In Java and JavaScript, primitive types and classes behave differently. (Python and Ruby don’t have primitive values, but use immutable instances to simulate them.) When a primitive value is assigned to another variable or passed to a function or method, any changes made to the other variable won’t be reflected in the original, as shown in the Java code in Example 5-1. Example 5-1. Assigning primitive variables doesn’t share memory in Java int x = 10; int y = x; y = 20; System.out.println(x); // prints 10 However, let’s take a look at what happens when an instance of a class is assigned to another variable or passed to a function or method. (The code in Example 5-2 is written in Python, but you can find similar code for Java, JavaScript, and Ruby in the examples/language_pointer_examples directory.) Example 5-2. Passing a class instance into a function in Python class Foo: def __init__(self, x): self.x = x def outer(): f = Foo(10) inner1(f) print(f.x) inner2(f) print(f.x) g = None inner2(g) print(g is None) def inner1(f): f.x = 20 def inner2(f): f = Foo(30) outer() Running this code prints the following output: 20 20 True That’s because the following scenarios are true in Java, Python, JavaScript, and Ruby: If you pass an instance of a class to a function and you change the value of a field, the change is reflected in the variable that was passed in. If you reassign the parameter, the change is not reflected in the variable that was passed in. If you pass nil/null/None for a parameter value, setting the parameter itself to a new value doesn’t modify the variable in the calling function. Some people explain this behavior by saying that class instances are passed by reference in these languages. This is untrue. If they were being passed by reference, the second and third scenarios would change the variable in the calling function. These languages are always pass-by-value, just as in Go. What you are seeing is that every instance of a class in these languages is implemented as a pointer. When a class instance is passed to a function or method, the value being copied is the pointer to the instance. Since outer and inner1 are referring to the same memory, changes made to fields in f in inner1 are reflected in the variable in outer. When inner2 reassigns f to a new class instance, this creates a separate instance and does not affect the variable in outer. When you use a pointer variable or parameter in Go, you see the exact same behaviors. The difference between Go and these languages is that Go gives you the choice to use pointers or values for both primitives and structs. Most of the time, you should use a value. Values make it easier to understand how and when your data is modified. A secondary benefit is that using values reduces the amount of work that the garbage collector has to do. I’ll talk about that in “Reducing the Garbage Collector’s Workload”.

title: Emptying a Map
text: Emptying a Map The clear function that you saw in “Emptying a Slice” works on maps also. A cleared map has its length set to zero, unlike a cleared slice. The following code: m := map[string]int{ "hello": 5, "world": 10, } fmt.Println(m, len(m)) clear(m) fmt.Println(m, len(m)) prints out: map[hello:5 world:10] 2 map[] 0

title: Emptying a Slice
text: Emptying a Slice Go 1.21 added a clear function that takes in a slice and sets all of the slice’s elements to their zero value. The length of the slice remains unchanged. The following code: s := []string{"first", "second", "third"} fmt.Println(s, len(s)) clear(s) fmt.Println(s, len(s)) prints out: [first second third] 3 [ ] 3 (Remember, the zero value for a string is an empty string ""!)

title: Finding Concurrent Data Access Problems with the Data Race Detector
text: Finding Concurrent Data Access Problems with the Data Race Detector Even with Go’s built-in support for concurrency, bugs still happen. It’s easy to accidentally reference a variable from two different goroutines without acquiring a lock. The computer science term for this is a data race. To help find these sorts of bugs, Go includes a race detector. It isn’t guaranteed to find every single data race in your code, but if it finds one, you should put proper locks around what it finds. Look at a simple example in the file examples/race/race.go : func getCounter() int { var counter int var wg sync.WaitGroup for range 5 { wg.Go(func() { for range 1000 { counter++ } }) } wg.Wait() return counter } This code launches five goroutines, has each of them update a shared counter variable 1,000 times, and then returns the result. You’d expect it to be 5,000, so let’s verify this with a unit test in examples/race/race_test.go : func TestGetCounter(t *testing.T) { counter := getCounter() if counter != 5000 { t.Error("unexpected counter:", counter) } } If you run go test a few times, you’ll see that sometimes it passes, but most of the time it fails with an error message like this: unexpected counter: 3673 The problem is that there’s a data race in the code. In a program this simple, the cause is obvious: multiple goroutines are trying to update counter simultaneously, and some of their updates are lost. In more complicated programs, these sorts of races are harder to see. Let’s see what the data race detector does. Use the flag -race with go test to enable it: $ go test -race ================== WARNING: DATA RACE Read at 0x00c000128070 by goroutine 10: test_examples/race.getCounter.func1() test_examples/race/race.go:12 +0x45 Previous write at 0x00c000128070 by goroutine 8: test_examples/race.getCounter.func1() test_examples/race/race.go:12 +0x5b The traces make it clear that the line counter++ is the source of your problems. Warning Some people try to fix race conditions by inserting “sleeps” into their code, trying to space out access to the variable that’s being accessed by multiple goroutines. This is a bad idea. Doing so might eliminate the problem in some cases, but the code is still wrong and will fail in some situations. You can also use the -race flag when you build your programs. This creates a binary that includes the data race detector and that reports any races it finds to the console. This allows you to find data races in code that doesn’t have tests. If the data race detector is so useful, why isn’t it enabled all the time for testing and production? A binary with -race enabled runs approximately 10 times slower than a normal binary. That isn’t a problem for test suites that take a second to run, but for large test suites that take several minutes, a 10× slowdown reduces productivity. For more information on the data race detector, check out its official documentation.

title: Functions
text: Functions

title: Functions Are Values
text: Functions Are Values Just as in many other languages, functions in Go are values. The type of a function is built out of the keyword func and the types of the parameters and return values. This combination is called the signature of the function. Any function that has the exact same number and types of parameters and return values meets the type signature. Since functions are values, you can declare a function variable: var myFuncVariable func(string) int You can assign myFuncVariable any function that has a single parameter of type string and returns a single value of type int. Here’s a longer example: func f1(a string) int { return len(a) } func f2(a string) int { total := 0 for _, v := range a { total += int(v) } return total } func main() { var myFuncVariable func(string) int myFuncVariable = f1 result := myFuncVariable("Hello") fmt.Println(result) myFuncVariable = f2 result = myFuncVariable("Hello") fmt.Println(result) } You can run this program on The Go Playground. The output is: 5 500 The default zero value for a function variable is nil. Attempting to run a function variable with a nil value results in a panic (which is covered in the Panic Recover section). Having functions as values allows you to do some clever things, such as build a simple calculator using functions as values in a map. Let’s see how this works. The following code is available on The Go Playground. First, create a set of functions that all have the same signature: func add(i int, j int) int { return i + j } func sub(i int, j int) int { return i - j } func mul(i int, j int) int { return i * j } func div(i int, j int) int { return i / j } Next, create a map to associate a math operator with each function: var opMap = map[string]func(int, int) int{ "+": add, "-": sub, "*": mul, "/": div, } Finally, try out the calculator with a few expressions: func main() { expressions := [][]string{ {"2", "+", "3"}, {"2", "-", "3"}, {"2", "*", "3"}, {"2", "/", "3"}, {"2", "%", "3"}, {"two", "+", "three"}, {"5"}, } for _, expression := range expressions { if len(expression) != 3 { fmt.Println("invalid expression:", expression) continue } p1, err := strconv.Atoi(expression[0]) if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) continue } op := expression[1] opFunc, ok := opMap[op] if !ok { fmt.Println("unsupported operator:", op) continue } p2, err := strconv.Atoi(expression[2]) if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) continue } result := opFunc(p1, p2) fmt.Println(result) } } The strconv.Atoi function in the standard library converts a string to an int. The second value returned by this function is an error. As shown earlier, every time you call a function that returns an error, check the returned error value. If it is not nil, handle the error. In this case, we print out the error and skip the rest of the for loop. You''ll use op as the key to the opMap map and assign the value associated with the key to the variable opFunc. The type of opFunc is func(int, int) int. If there wasn’t a function in the map associated with the provided key, print an error message and skip the rest of the loop. Then call the function assigned to the opFunc variable with the p1 and p2 variables that you decoded earlier. Calling a function in a variable looks just like calling a function directly. When you run this program, you can see the simple calculator at work: 5 -1 6 0 unsupported operator: % strconv.Atoi: parsing "two": invalid syntax invalid expression: [5] Note Don’t write fragile programs. The core logic for this example is relatively short. Of the 22 lines inside the for loop, 6 of them implement the actual algorithm, and the other 16 are for error checking and data validation. You might be tempted to not validate incoming data or check errors, but doing so produces unstable, unmaintainable code. Error handling is what separates the professionals from the amateurs. Function Type Declarations Just as you can use the type keyword to define a struct, you can use it to define a function type, too. Take a look: type opFuncType func(int,int) int You can then rewrite the opMap declaration to look like this: var opMap = map[string]opFuncType { // same as before } You don’t have to modify the functions at all. Any function that has two input parameters of type int and a single return value of type int automatically meets the type and can be assigned as a value in the map. What’s the advantage of declaring a function type? One use is documentation. It’s useful to give something a name if you’re going to refer to it multiple times. You will see another use in the related discussion.
